text: Secret rotation means periodically changing a secret's value automatically, on a schedule, rather than setting it once and leaving it unchanged indefinitely. Rotation doesn't prevent a leak -- a secret can still end up in a build log, a misconfigured public repo, or an old laptop backup, no matter how good your rotation policy is. What it changes is what happens after that leak, in the gap before anyone notices it.

Without rotation, a leaked password nobody detects stays valid indefinitely -- it could be used a day, a month, or a year later. With rotation, that same leaked password stops working the next time rotation runs, whether anyone caught the leak or not. A credential rotated every 30 days has, at most, a 30-day window of usefulness to someone who stole it unnoticed.

Rotation limits how long a leaked secret works. Access policies limit who can get at the secret in the first place, governed by least privilege: a secret should be readable only by the specific application or service identity that actually needs it, never by an entire team or resource group, even though broader access is often more convenient to set up once and forget about.

In both Azure Key Vault and AWS's secret services, that's the default posture to design toward -- each secret has its own small list of who can read it, built from what's actually needed. A broad grant, giving a whole team read-all access because it's easier than scoping individually, turns one compromised account into access to every secret in the vault.

Rotation and least-privilege access cover different failure modes, not the same one -- access policies try to prevent an unauthorized read, rotation assumes a leak slips through anyway and makes sure it expires. That closes out secrets management. Next, Chapter 5: what Cloud Security Posture Management actually catches, starting with the misconfigurations secrets alone don't fix.
